"When a part of it is cut off ...there will be a replacement, it's only natural," he said. Dujana denied being involved in the Marriott Hotel attack. Bush and then-British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who he says are not giving Muslims the chance to be in power. Dujana studied in Pakistan and fought in Afghanistan from 1988 to 1991. He told CNN that he met al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden in Afghanistan during the fight against Soviet occupation. At the time, bin Laden was a field commander and he was an ordinary soldier, he said. Dujana said bin Laden was well respected then and helped him and others realize that it was permissible to kill people to defend Islam. "I didn't read it in the Quran," he said. " It's based on the teachings of our teachers, clerics, especially what Osama bin Laden first said." "Because of America's arrogance, many in the Muslim world know, believe, it's permissible to kill American soldiers. It's halal; it's permitted," he said. The court declared Jemaah Islamiyah a terrorist organization Monday and ordered it to pay 10 million rupiah ($1,088). Around the same time Dujana was captured last June, authorities also apprehended Jemaah Islamiyah's leader, known simply as Zarkasih. A verdict on his case is expected soon. Last week, two other top Jemaah Islamiyah leaders -- Dr. Agus Purwanto and Abdur Rohim -- were brought to Indonesia following their arrest in Malaysia. Both are being investigated for their possible role in fomenting violence in Poso. Terrorism expert Sidney Jones says Abdur Rohim is believed to have replaced Zarkasih as Jemaah Islamiyah leader. "It is another major blow to Jemaah Islamiyah, but difficult to tell what the impact will be," Jones told CNN via e-mail last week. "It could embolden a more militant faction. [It] could also lead to some serious reassessment within the organization about its future." E-mail to a friend . CNN's Kathy Quiano contributed to this report.

JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) -- An Indonesian court has sentenced the alleged military commander of an al Qaeda-linked terror network to 15 years in prison. Abu Dujana is suspected of plotting attacks on the Australian Embassy and the J.W. Marriott hotel in Jakarta.

Dujana is the alleged leader of the military wing of Jemaah Islamiyah, a group believed to have ties to al Qaeda and which seeks to establish a Muslim "superstate" spanning much of Southeast Asia. A slight, wiry man, Dujana stands accused of direct involvement in the 2002 Bali nightclub bombings, which claimed the lives of more than 200 people, predominantly Western tourists. He is likewise suspected of orchestrating subsequent attacks on the Australian Embassy and the J.W. Marriott hotel, both located in the Indonesian capital.

Authorities further allege that Dujana bears responsibility for the ongoing violence in Poso, on Indonesia's eastern island of Sulawesi, where clashes between Muslim and Christian communities erupt periodically and have at times proven fatal. Police maintain that Jemaah Islamiyah has dispatched armed militants to the region.

On Monday, the court found Dujana guilty of illegally possessing firearms and explosives, as well as harboring suspected terrorists. His legal team indicated they may appeal the ruling.

Following his arrest last June after a four-year manhunt, Dujana acknowledged to CNN that he served as Jemaah Islamiyah's military chief, though he claimed this role began only after the attacks on Western targets had already occurred. He characterized Jemaah Islamiyah to CNN as "an underground organization" that "will continue to exist and continue to move on with its plans" to establish an Islamic state governed by Sharia law, notwithstanding his own capture. "When a part of it is cut off... there will be a replacement—it's only natural," he remarked.

Dujana denied any involvement in the Marriott Hotel attack, though he told CNN he had assisted fugitive suspect Noordin Top in planning the assault, meeting with him both before and after the devastating blast that killed 12 people and injured 150. "It's true, I did have a meeting with Noordin before the Marriott bombing, but that doesn't mean I was involved in the attack," he said. "In that meeting, we were simply aligning our views with each other—there was absolutely no discussion about planning any bombing."

Throughout his CNN interview, Dujana readily espoused messages of hatred, declaring all Westerners legitimate targets on account of the actions of leaders such as U.S. President George W. Bush and then-British Prime Minister Tony Blair, whom he accused of denying Muslims the opportunity to hold power.

Dujana studied in Pakistan and fought in Afghanistan from 1988 to 1991. He told CNN that he encountered al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden in Afghanistan during the resistance against Soviet occupation—bin Laden then serving as a field commander while Dujana was but an ordinary soldier. He recalled that bin Laden commanded considerable respect at the time and helped him and others come to believe that killing in defense of Islam was permissible. "I didn't read it in the Quran," he explained. "It's based on the teachings of our teachers, clerics—especially what Osama bin Laden first said. Because of America's arrogance, many in the Muslim world know, believe, it's permissible to kill American soldiers. It's halal; it's permitted."

The court also declared Jemaah Islamiyah a terrorist organization on Monday and ordered it to pay a fine of 10 million rupiah ($1,088).

Around the time of Dujana's capture last June, authorities also apprehended Jemaah Islamiyah's leader, known simply as Zarkasih; a verdict in his case is expected shortly. Last week, two additional senior Jemaah Islamiyah figures—Dr. Agus Purwanto and Abdur Rohim—were extradited to Indonesia following their arrest in Malaysia. Both are under investigation for their possible roles in inciting the violence in Poso.

Terrorism expert Sidney Jones noted that Abdur Rohim is believed to have succeeded Zarkasih as head of Jemaah Islamiyah. "It is another major blow to Jemaah Islamiyah, but difficult to tell what the impact will be," Jones told CNN via e-mail last week. "It could embolden a more militant faction. [It] could also lead to some serious reassessment within the organization about its future."

E-mail to a friend.

CNN's Kathy Quiano contributed to this report.

An Indonesian court has sentenced Abu Dujana, the alleged military commander of the al Qaeda-linked Jemaah Islamiyah network, to 15 years in prison after finding him guilty of illegally possessing firearms and explosives and harboring suspected terrorists. The ruling, handed down by the South Jakarta District Court, represents one of the most significant legal actions taken against the leadership of Jemaah Islamiyah (JI), a militant organization believed responsible for a series of deadly attacks across the region.

Prosecutors had sought a longer sentence, presenting evidence that linked Dujana to some of the most notorious terrorist incidents in Indonesia's recent history. The verdict has been hailed by security officials as a milestone in Indonesia's broader campaign against terrorism, which has intensified since the Bali bombings prompted a major crackdown on militant networks operating within the world's most populous Muslim-majority nation. Indonesian authorities, often working alongside international partners including Australia and the United States, have arrested and prosecuted dozens of suspected JI members in the years since, weakening the network's operational capacity and disrupting numerous plots.

However, the case has also renewed concerns about the resilience of Jemaah Islamiyah and its enduring ideological commitment to establishing an Islamic superstate spanning Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and other parts of Southeast Asia. Analysts caution that while the sentencing of high-profile figures like Dujana represents important tactical victories, the broader challenge of countering JI's ideological appeal and its deep roots in certain religious and educational institutions remains far from resolved. # Indonesian Court Sentences Jemaah Islamiyah Military Leader Abu Dujana to 15 Years

**JAKARTA** — An Indonesian court has sentenced Abu Dujana, the alleged military commander of the Southeast Asian militant network Jemaah Islamiyah (JI), to 15 years in prison, capping a closely watched trial that shed new light on the organization's structure, ideology, and international connections.

## The Verdict

Judges at the South Jakarta District Court found Abu Dujana, whose real name is Yassin Syawal, guilty of harboring fugitives, possessing illegal firearms, and providing material support to militant operations. While prosecutors had sought a longer sentence, the court determined that direct evidence linking him to specific bombing plots was insufficient for harsher terrorism charges, though his leadership role within JI's military wing was affirmed.

Abu Dujana, captured in a raid in Central Java in 2007, had served as the head of JI's *askari* (military) division — a position that made him one of the most senior operational figures apprehended since the group's founding.

## Jemaah Islamiyah's Ideology

Jemaah Islamiyah emerged in the late 1980s and 1990s from a network of Indonesian and Malaysian militants inspired by a vision of establishing an Islamic caliphate across Southeast Asia, encompassing Indonesia, Malaysia, the southern Philippines, and Singapore. The group's founders, Abdullah Sungkar and Abu Bakar Bashir, drew heavily on Salafi-jihadist thought, blending it with regional grievances and networks forged during the anti-Soviet jihad in Afghanistan.

JI has been linked to a string of devastating attacks, most notably the 2002 Bali bombings that killed 202 people, as well as the 2003 Marriott Hotel bombing in Jakarta and the 2004 Australian Embassy bombing. The group's ideology called for violent jihad against Western targets and secular governments in the region, which it viewed as obstacles to establishing Islamic rule.

## Ties to Osama bin Laden

Court testimony and intelligence assessments presented during the trial reinforced long-held assessments that JI maintained operational and ideological links to al-Qaeda. Several JI members, including senior figures who trained in Afghan camps during the 1980s and 1990s, forged personal relationships with Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda's leadership.

Prosecutors noted that JI's structure and tactics — including its use of cell-based organization and suicide bombing operations — mirrored al-Qaeda's playbook, and that financial and logistical support flowed between the networks at various points. Abu Dujana himself was described in court documents as part of a generation of JI operatives whose ideological formation was shaped directly by exposure to bin Laden's global jihadist vision during the Afghan conflict era.

## Analyst Reaction: Sidney Jones

Sidney Jones, a leading terrorism analyst specializing in Southeast Asian militancy, offered a measured response to the sentencing, cautioning against viewing it as a decisive blow to JI's networks.

"The sentence reflects the limits of what prosecutors could prove in court, not necessarily the scope of what Abu Dujana actually did," Jones said. "He was a central figure in maintaining JI's military infrastructure — training, weapons, safe houses — even as the group publicly claimed to have renounced violence."

Jones emphasized that Abu Dujana's capture and trial exposed the resilience of JI's underlying networks despite years of counterterrorism pressure. "What this case really shows is that JI didn't disappear after Bali — it fractured, went quieter, but the ideological commitment and the personal networks remained intact," she said. "The real danger is assuming that a court verdict, however significant, equals the end of the threat."

She also noted that the relatively lighter sentence could fuel internal debate among Indonesian security officials over whether existing anti-terrorism laws are adequate to prosecute senior militant figures whose roles are more organizational than directly operational.

## Broader Implications

The case underscores the ongoing challenge facing Indonesian authorities: dismantling a resilient militant network whose structure was deliberately designed for cellular secrecy and long-term survival, even as its most visible leaders are captured, tried, and imprisoned. Analysts like Jones continue to warn that splinter factions and ideological successors could carry JI's vision forward, even as its formal structure weakens.

# Indonesian Terror Suspect Abu Dujana Convicted, Sentenced to 15 Years

**JAKARTA, Indonesia** — An Indonesian court on Thursday convicted alleged Jemaah Islamiyah military commander Abu Dujana on terrorism charges, sentencing him to 15 years in prison in a case that has offered rare insight into the inner workings of the al Qaeda-linked network blamed for some of Southeast Asia's deadliest bombings.

Abu Dujana, whose real name is Ainul Bahri, was found guilty of harboring fugitives, possessing illegal firearms, and providing military training to militants — charges connected to his alleged role as the operational military leader of Jemaah Islamiyah, the organization responsible for the 2002 Bali bombings that killed 202 people.

In an exclusive interview with CNN prior to his trial, Abu Dujana admitted to his membership in Jemaah Islamiyah and acknowledged his role in training militants and storing weapons for the organization. He described his involvement in the group's military wing, offering an unusual glimpse into the hierarchy and operations of a network that has been blamed for a string of attacks across the region since the early 2000s.

However, Abu Dujana firmly denied any involvement in the 2003 bombing of the JW Marriott Hotel in Jakarta, an attack that killed 12 people and wounded more than 150. That bombing, along with a series of other attacks, has been attributed to Jemaah Islamiyah's most militant faction, allegedly led by bomb-making expert Noordin Mohammed Top, who remains at large.

Prosecutors had sought a longer sentence, but the panel of judges said they took into account what they described as Abu Dujana's cooperation with investigators during the trial. Defense attorneys have not indicated whether they plan to appeal the verdict.

Abu Dujana's arrest last year was hailed by Indonesian and Western counterterrorism officials as a significant blow to Jemaah Islamiyah's operational capabilities. Analysts say his capture, along with a wave of subsequent arrests, has substantially degraded the network's ability to plan and execute large-scale attacks.

In the months following his detention, Indonesian authorities have arrested several other senior Jemaah Islamiyah figures, according to police statements. Among those apprehended was Zarkasih, identified by investigators as the group's overall leader, who was captured in a separate raid shortly after Abu Dujana's arrest. Indonesian police have described the arrests as part of a broader crackdown that has disrupted the network's leadership structure and financing operations.

Counterterrorism experts caution, however, that despite these successes, Jemaah Islamiyah has not been fully dismantled. Splinter cells and radicalized individuals inspired by the group's ideology continue to pose a threat, they say, particularly given the continued freedom of key figures like Noordin Mohammed Top.

Indonesia has emerged as a key battleground in Southeast Asia's fight against Islamist militancy since the 2002 Bali attacks prompted a major overhaul of the country's counterterrorism apparatus, backed by significant assistance from the United States and Australia.

The trial and conviction of Abu Dujana is expected to be followed by additional prosecutions of Jemaah Islamiyah members currently in custody, as Indonesian authorities continue to pursue those believed responsible for the country's deadliest terrorist attacks.

*CNN's Jakarta bureau contributed to this report.*
